Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER

Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: May we call [Dr C], please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Dr C] (sworn)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
Could you please state your full name for the record?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I'm [Dr C].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Dr C], may I invite you to project your answers to the jury, although I'll be asking them in the first place at least.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you tell the jury of your occupational status, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I'm a consultant paediatrician at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you confirm that that was your role back in 2015?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes, that was.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. I think you appreciate that you've been invited here this morning to answer questions that concern a patient within the hospital, a baby by the name of [Baby E] --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- who, as I'm sure you know, was born, together with his twin brother [Baby F], on 29 July 2015?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Prior to answering questions from the police in the preparation of the making of a witness statement, were you given the opportunity to remind yourself of some of the details of the clinical records pertaining to that patient?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes, I was.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: May I assure you that insofar as we go to any such records in this courtroom today, they will be displayed on the screen there, just to your right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Okay.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If you wish to see any more, we have them there to be produced at request.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We understand, and could you confirm, that you were the on-call consultant for the neonatal department on the 3rd and 4 August 2015?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: When on call, where would you reside?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Normally, I would stay in the hospital until about 7 or 8 pm that night, and once I was happy that all of the patients were stable and had an appropriate management plan, then the usual practice is that consultants are on call from home, but I live too far away, so I stay in the hospital accommodation, which is about 5 to 10 minutes' walk from the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Can you confirm that you were on site, by which I mean --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: It's within the hospital site, but it's at the opposite end of the site.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Forgive me, I didn't make myself clear. I was inviting you to tell us whether you were actually within the unit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I wasn't within the unit at the time after about 7 or 8 pm.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But prior to that --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Prior to that I had been and I would have had a handover from the junior doctors, so I would have been aware of all of the children on the neonatal unit and the paediatric unit and a summary of their clinical condition before I left the building.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you for that.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm going to put something on screen now and ask the assistance of Mr Murphy, please. If you could take us to tile number 128, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This recreation, this presentation here, [Dr C], sets out a chronology of key events and entries made in the records. You can see the date here, Monday, 3 August 2015, behind which we have uploaded PDF reproductions of the actual notes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So you'll see there a description and if we go behind it, you'll see here an example of a note made by a junior colleague, Dr Thomas, in the upper part of the page, and a little further down, your colleague Dr Harkness, who I think you'll able to confirm was the registrar on duty at that time.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes, he was.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you recall having communication and interaction with Dr Harkness on this date about the baby [Baby E]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I do. It's not a particularly clear memory given the amount of time that's passed, but I do remember two phone calls and then subsequently attending the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Before we get to the phone calls, do you remember, and say if you don't, any discussion, exchange of information between you and Dr Harkness whilst you were on the unit prior to you going to the accommodation that you described already?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: No. He would have been the night doctor, which meant he wouldn't have arrived until about 8.30, so I don't think I would have spoken to him prior to the telephone calls, and if I did I certainly don't recall that.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. If, Mr Murphy, we go to the bottom of the pages available on this particular screen. Forgive me, I'm
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: looking for -- towards the bottom of page J2555. So scroll up a little.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We have an entry from Dr Harkness, timed about 22.10 hours, which gives a description of his observations. If we scroll down to the bottom of this entry, we'll see it concludes with a note of him communicating with you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So let's just confirm that. We see, to the bottom of that entry, I think it's D/W, which is a doctor's abbreviation, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes, it means "discussed with".
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Discussed with] [a standard abbreviation].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: [Dr C] happy with plan."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes, his writing is not the easiest to understand, but it does say "happy with plan". He contacted me by telephone, explained the clinical situation, and his planned management plan, and I agreed that that seemed the appropriate thing to do. I always check, when I speak with one of the junior doctors on the phone, that they're happy with it just being a call for discussion and advice or whether they do want me to come in because sometimes they're not always confident enough to ask that, and he did confirm that he was happy with the situation and didn't need me to physically attend the unit at that point.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's scroll back up and let's look at the recorded clinical situation, as you've described it, as noted by Dr Harkness. "ATSP"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: That's "asked to see patient".
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So he was asked to see the patient. It reads?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: "Re gastric", which means the stomach bleed.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then thereafter, he's noted "large..."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: "... very slightly bile-stained aspirate 30 minutes ago.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sudden large volume of fresh blood, approximately 14ml, as aspirate."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Pausing there. Between the words "blood" and the numerals "14", is that the abbreviation for approximately?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I think it is but I'm not 100% certain.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Dr Harkness will be with us tomorrow, so he will be able to assist.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: When that blood is an aspirate, it's usually not all blood, it's the stomach contents, the aspirate, and it all looks red because it's mixed with blood, but it wouldn't always be 14ml of just pure blood, if that makes sense.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We understand.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: 14ml of volume, not all blood, but --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR C: Some of it will be stomach contents.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: -- and other dilutants?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you. The background, I think this is a background to the baby --
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: It is.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: -- rather than the event?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. It's reversed end-diastolic flow, which is the blood flow from the placenta to the baby. If a baby has reduced enddiastolic flow they haven't had as good perfusion from the placenta, a transfer of blood and nutrients, as they perhaps might have done. And then the following one is IUGR, which is intrauterine growth restriction, which means the baby hadn't grown as well in the womb as we would have liked, which is a consequence of the reduced placental blood flow.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Both of those factors mean that is the baby is more likely to have a problem with their bowel, known as necrotising enterocolitis or NEC, which is why Dr Harkness has noted them as being relevant. He's put:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Re-screened for increased oxygen requirement yesterday."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That means screening for infection, doing blood tests, looking for infection and giving the baby antibiotics. And he notes that the CRP and inflammatory marker is less than 1, which is a sign that infection is unlikely, but we do always tend to be cautious
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: with small babies, and then that he's opening his bowels, which makes NEC a bit less likely.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So to review those four notes under the sub-heading "Background", the first two are indicators of a heightened risk for NEC?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But numbers 3 and 4 are indicators inconsistent with the presence of NEC?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Move on to the next entry, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: That's mean blood pressure 48, which is a good blood pressure for a baby of his size. Capillary refill time of less than 2, which is a measure of the baby's perfusion and circulation, which is normal.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Heart rate, I think it says 140 to 100, which is again within sort of normal ranges. And sats 100% in 23% inhaled oxygen, which is a normal or very good saturation rate, but requiring a small amount of oxygen; room air is 21% oxygen.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. If Mr Murphy could take us further down the page or on to the next page, more accurately. The same note, effectively. Could you continue to assist?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. That's O/E, which means "on examination". There's then some statements about the baby which says:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Alert, pink, well perfused, capillary refill time less than 2."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's a sort of standard thing we look at when first examining a baby, to get a sense of their overall clinical condition, which looks normal and healthy in that assessment.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Heart rate is normal. There's then a picture of some lungs with a line through, which means that the lung sounds and the breath sounds were normal -- actually I wonder if this first one is HS, "heart sounds normal", it's difficult to tell from Dr Harkness' writing.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Abdo [which is short for abdomen] soft, not distended, and bowel sounds present."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Again, which is a normal examination.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the plus symbol next to the letters BS, you interpret that as present?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: That's sort of standard medical documentation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: It says:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "AF normotensive."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: AF is the anterior fontanelle, the soft spot on the baby's head. That's used as part of our assessment to see whether or not their circulation is okay, which it looks like from this assessment. Also if it's bulging it suggests there may be a problem like meningitis, which isn't mentioned on this assessment.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What does --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Normotensive is an expression that means that the blood pressure and the pressure is normal. So if a baby was clinically dehydrated or had low blood pressure, their fontanelle might be sunken.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Which is the opposite to normotensive in this context?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Next?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: "Femorals ++."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Femorals are one of the pulses which are present in the groin and because of babies' fat distribution they're one of the central pulses that are easiest to feel. Because of babies' necks being quite thick, we don't often feel for carotid pulses in the neck in the way that you would do in adults. And the two pluses means both of the femorals were palpable, which means you could feel them.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Finally for this description?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: The triangle means diagnosis. So he said:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "GI [which is gastrointestinal] bleed, [query] cause."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And then he has moved on to a management plan.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Before we consider the plan, having kindly taken us through Dr Harkness' notes, do you recognise that as the clinical situation, to use your phrase, I think, that he conveyed to you by telephone?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And thereafter, he proposed a plan in response to that clinical situation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Which was, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: IV ranitidine, which is an anti-acid medicine.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: GI bleeds in small babies can often be due to their stomach acid, so we sometimes use anti-acid medicines.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: To add in metronidazole, which is an antibiotic that we use in cases of NEC, and in the brackets he's written "At risk of NEC" afterwards.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Again, the examination doesn't particularly support or doesn't support NEC at all at this point, but sometimes babies take a while to develop clear clinical signs and if we don't start treatment early then by the time they've developed clear signs things have deteriorated too far so we often tend to be cautious and start things like antibiotics early.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: He's then written:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Close observation and for a repeat full blood count in the morning."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Which is a blood test that measures, amongst other things, the haemoglobin, the red blood cells. If someone's had a bleed you can't measure their full blood count too soon because if you lose a volume of your circulating blood initially, if you check your full blood count, it will be exactly the same, you've got the same concentration of blood, it's just there's less of it. If you wait a few hours and the body's had time to adjust you'll be able to have an indication of how much blood was lost. So that's why that wasn't done immediately at the time and the plan was to do it the following morning.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you for that. Again, does that note accord with the plan as communicated to you by Dr Harkness?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes, it does.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And did you deem it an appropriate response and a way forward having considered the clinical situation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. It was the same thing I would have done if I'd been present on the ward at the time.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. I think a little earlier, when first telling us about receiving this call and your dialogue with Dr Harkness, I think you told us that you believe that you volunteered to attend to assist if he so wished.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. That's always my standard practice when having phone calls from juniors when I'm not present. And even when discussing patients, if I'm in the hospital but not physically at the patient's bedside, I always check whether they are happy with just a discussion and advice or whether they do want me to actually physically see the patient. Because sometimes they don't always like to ask you but when you volunteer they may say that they do want you to see the patient.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There's nothing in the records to suggest, nothing from your memory, to suggest that on this occasion he did so wish and you did so attend?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. From what I recall of the conversation, he declined and said he was happy and if he had said he wanted me to attend, then I have never refused to attend when I've been asked, so I would have done so straightaway.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. We can see that Dr Harkness noted all of this, noted it at 22.10.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's not to say it all happened at 22.10 --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- but some time a little before that time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then his note moves forward to 23.00 hours. If we go to the bottom of that note we can see that he's endorsed here:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Dr C], happy with plan again."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that note tends to suggest that a second conversation with Dr Harkness -- do you recall such a second conversation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Vaguely. But I would need to rely on the medical notes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't remember the detail of that conversation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: From the vague recollection you have, are you able to say whether the second conversation with Dr Harkness was faceto-face or --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: That was through the telephone.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Telephone again. So a second call?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: He's noted these events and at 23.00 -- and can you help us with what it was that he was recording at this point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. He's noted a further GI blood loss and a plus, which means "and" in this situation, desaturation to 70%. That means a drop in the oxygen saturations from 100%, which it was previously, to 70%.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Upon that being communicated to you, how would that affect your assessment of the clinical situation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: That's a baby that needs at that point immediate medical assistance, which is what Dr Harkness is giving to them at the time. He would have updated me after he'd done that and the baby was then stable again.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's go through the other factors of the clinical situation before looking at the nature of the assistance provided. My error. Apologies.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Next note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: He's written:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "13ml bloodstained fluid from the NG tube."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Which is the nasogastric tube, the tube that goes from the nose into the stomach, which was on free drainage, and that means that the end is left open so any fluid in the stomach can come up the tube. Again, this would be a mixture of blood and stomach aspirates.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The fact that this is written as bloodstained rather than blood as the previous one does suggest that it was maybe slightly pinker rather than redder, but I obviously wasn't there to see the aspirate at the time.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then BP blood pressure is stable with a mean blood pressure of 43, which again is very good. And a heart rate of 140 to 160.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Pausing there, going back to the last line, the 13ml of bloodstained fluid from NGT on free drainage, on your interpretation of that note does that tend to suggest that that fluid was manually aspirated from the baby or did it --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: No, I think it would have come up the tube spontaneously or been found in the bag that was connected to the tube by the nurse who was looking after the baby.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So there is the further blood loss, there is a desaturation to 70%, and that note that we've just considered twice. And then you were taking us through the other readings. Could you help us with those again?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: The blood pressure is stable with a mean blood pressure of 43, which is a very good blood pressure for a baby of [Baby E]'s size. His heart was 140 to 160, which is normal. A baby who's losing a significant amount of blood would tend to develop a fast heart rate and a low blood pressure if they were losing a lot of blood and needed fluid resuscitation at that point.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did that --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: At that point that hasn't happened.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So Dr Harkness' next note, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: "Saturations remained 60 to 70% [which should be in the 90s] in 100% inhaled oxygen. Making a good respiratory effort and crying."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So this suggests that he's applied 100% oxygen or the nursing staff have applied 100% oxygen to [Baby E], but his saturations haven't responded to that, which normally a baby who was only needing 23% oxygen earlier to have saturations of 100% to now need 100% oxygen and still not be maintaining their saturations suggested that something dramatic has changed in their clinical condition.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It says he's making a good respiratory effort and crying, so it suggests that it's not a problem with his breathing effort that's caused -- that's making his oxygen saturations be low.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I know this is obvious to you, but you suggested something dramatic has happened.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was that a negative or a positive trend?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: A negative trend.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thereafter, (inaudible: coughing) plan of action, as it were.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. The first step is to replace the losses, so he's given 20ml per kilogram of 0.9% saline, which is a salt water solution that we use to replace babies who are having fluid losses. He has lost quite a lot of fluid in the aspirates and in the blood, so the plan is to replace that. Again, as I mentioned earlier, we like to try and do things proactively before it becomes a problem. So although his heart rate and blood pressure are still okay, we don't want to wait until that becomes a problem before giving him some more fluid. So that was done proactively by Dr Harkness.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The second item is "strict fluid balance". That means the nursing staff noting all the volumes of fluid that the baby gets in, which would be their IV fluids, it may be drug medicines, it may be, if they are having any milk feeds, which he wouldn't have been doing by this stage, that that's all noted. And again, any fluid losses are noted very strictly, so all the gastric aspirates, they then weigh the nappies so we can calculate the volume of urine passed, and then calculations are done every few hours to make sure that the baby's input and output are relatively closely matched and can be adjusted if things need to be.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: To review that, in consequence of that which had been observed, a yet more strict regime of observance of fluid input and output --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- was suggested?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. Normally, we would just document whether babies are weeing or not, but if they need a closer eye keeping then we weigh the nappies and document the exact volume of urine that's passed.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Next, is that:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "For elective intubation with drugs"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. That means putting a tube in the baby's windpipe and taking over their breathing for them, which is something that we do if a baby's either working too hard with their breathing or their breathing is not having the required effect, which in this case, where his saturations are still low, he's not got good enough oxygenation, so we'd take over doing that for him.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Drugs means some sedative and pain-killing medicines that are just done to make that procedure more pleasant.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Just focusing upon the taking over his breathing for him, as you've just described it, this note indicates that he will be intubated --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- which is, we understand, could you confirm, to enable assistance with breathing?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's the method of assistance?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Intubating is the process of putting a tube into the windpipe. That would then be connected to a TP, which allows gas, oxygen and air to be delivered into the baby's lungs. Then once they're stable they'd be moved over on to a ventilator, a breathing machine, to do that for them.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Does this note, together with what memory you have of this conversation, inform you as to the type and degree of ventilatory support given to this baby at this time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: The plan would be to put the tube in and then get this baby stable on a ventilator for a period of time to work out what's going on and to start to see improvement.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that's the means of ventilation according to Dr Harkness' notes. His next entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: "CXR and AXR."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's a chest X-ray and abdominal X-ray. That's to look at the lungs to try and work out why [Baby E]'s now got low oxygen saturations, despite a reasonable breathing effort. And the Xray of the abdomen is to look for signs of NEC.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So these are X-ray investigations to try and assist in the identification of the cause?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes, and the chest X-ray will also be used to confirm that the ET tube, which is the breathing tube, is in the correct position and able to do its job properly.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So two results, two separate pieces of information: is the tube in where we wish it; and what's causing this problem?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. And "discussions with"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: "[Discussions with] surgeons with the X-rays."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: At this point, both Dr Harkness and I were thinking that [Baby E] possibly had NEC, which, if that were the case, treatment varies from bowel rest, which is not having any milk feeds along with IV fluids and antibiotics, up to needing surgical management, including removing the bowel. So the plan had been to ring the surgical team at Alder Hey, who would be able to review the X-rays electronically and discuss [Baby E]'s clinical condition and come up with a combined management plan of what we felt would be the most appropriate.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Just pausing with the X-rays for a moment, we've heard from other witnesses, could you tell us whether this was the position here with this patient, that a mobile X-ray device would be taken to the incubator?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That those treating the baby would look at the images taken through that device?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: The mobile X-ray machine has got a very small screen on it and we normally look at the X-ray at the time, just to check mainly the technical quality of the film, has the radiologist got every bit of the body that we want, does it look like the baby is not unduly rotated or twisted? And you can sometimes see obvious things on that small screen. It's not big enough or of a high enough resolution on the screen to give a formal report on the X-ray, so we will always review them again on our computer system on a higher quality monitor, but that takes time. The radiologist has to return the X-ray machine to the radiology department in the main hospital, they have to upload the cassette to be processed and then that has to appear on our electronic system, so that can take about 15 to 20 minutes for that to happen, which is why we have a quick look on the screen first. We also don't want them to leave the department if the film isn't of a good enough technical quality because we just ask them to repeat it immediately.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. So all this information was imparted to you by phone to where you were spending the night?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But for these events -- and as we understand it, at some point you left the residence and went to the NNU itself; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Are you able to recall with any precision when that was?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I've written in the note, the medical notes further on, that I arrived about 00.25, but I have no recollection of exactly when I arrived. I have no reason to doubt what I've written in the medical notes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's go to that note then and behind tile 163, Mr Murphy. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We can see this is described as a note written by you in retrospect at 01.30.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Which involves, amongst other things, the fact that CPR was commenced on this baby. Let's go to the note itself. It is dated and timed as indicated. We can see in the fifth line of the writing, the seventh or eighth line of the page itself:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "On my arrival, approx 00.25..."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that the note you were alluding to --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: That's the one I was referring to, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- a moment or two ago? So written in retrospect for reasons that will be obvious to us all. And you have begun by making notes. Would these be notes about things you observed upon arrival or notes about information shared with you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: They will probably be a combination of things that I've been told and things that I've observed.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. So, "GI haemorrhage". Did you observe that or were you told about it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I saw some of the syringes that contained bloodstained aspirates.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Discoloured abdomen", did you observe that or were you told about it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I don't think I did. When I arrived, Dr Harkness told me in quite a lot of detail about some very dark purple patches that he had seen on the abdomen and the unusual appearance of these.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Harkness can tell us about that. You've recorded the fact that information was imparted to you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes, I don't think by the time I saw [Baby E] that they were there because I've no recollection of that and I haven't documented that. I remember him telling me in quite an animated fashion because it was quite an unusual appearance, so I think if I'd seen it I would have definitely made a positive note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Next line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: "I&V [which stands for intubated and ventilated] for desats and bradys."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Which is a phenomenon that premature babies do, where they drop their oxygen saturations and they drop their heart rate, which we refer to as bradycardia, because we love to say everything in Latin and Greek rather than --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think you have to slow down a bit. Even just to listen to it, it's difficult, but for the people who are transcribing it -- all right?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You say things very quickly in Latin and Greek.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Somebody in a different place is noting your evidence and sometimes the words come out too quickly for the fingers.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I also talk quite quickly when I'm nervous.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's go back to that line:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "I&V for desats and bradys."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: So I&V stands for intubation and ventilation, which is the process of putting in a breathing tube and taking over the baby's breathing with a ventilator. Desats stands for desaturations, which is a drop in the oxygen saturations. And bradys stands for bradycardia, which is a drop in the heart rate.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Does all of that effectively reflect the clinical situation as reported to you by Dr Harkness in the last telephone conversation and corresponding set of notes that we've been through?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The next part of your note begins with:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "On my arrival, approximately 00.25..."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So are we now moving to observations and data that was present for you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: This would have been my own assessment.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Next line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: "SaO2" stands for oxygen saturations. I've written "80% in 100%". That means that [Baby E]'s saturations were 80% and he was having 100% oxygen. So those have improved since he's been put on the ventilator but are still not as good as we would like them to be.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's just remind ourselves of time. Dr Harkness' note was 23.40, his last note --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- 20 minutes before the other side of midnight, and this is now at or around 00.25?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So not as good as you would hope, but a good and improving trend?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Next?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: "AE" stands for air entry and that's when you listen to the baby's chest to check that the ventilator is getting a good amount of air into the lungs, or oxygen in this case. I have written "[equals] good bilaterally", which means that the breath sounds were equal on both sides and were the volume of gas transfer that we would expect. It shows that the ventilation is working well.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: For both lungs?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: For both lungs.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Next?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Heart rate. I have done a sort of wiggly equals sign, which means sort of approximately, so between 100 and 120.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Where does that fall in the desired range?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: That's a bit lower than it was previously, but that's still an acceptable heart rate.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then the mean blood pressure is 38, which again has dropped slightly, but is still acceptable. And the capillary refill time is between 2 and 3 seconds, which is slightly prolonged.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Which is indicative of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: The fact that [Baby E]'s perfusion is not as good as it was previously.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's to do with circulation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The next entry takes us to X-rays, does it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. It mentions that I'd looked at the chest X-ray on the X-ray machine. It shows the endotracheal tube, which is the breathing tube in a good position, that the nasogastric tube, the tip was in the stomach, which is where we'd want it to be. Then the next line doesn't refer to the X-ray. It says that [Baby E]'s on "cef", which is an antibiotic, cefotaxime and "met", another antibiotic, metronidazole, and I'd planned to add in teicoplanin, a third antibiotic, which covers for skin bacteria because he had, I believe, a long line and an intravenous line in situ, which are at risk of getting infections from skin bacteria but that we didn't have chance to give that before further events unfolded.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm not going to put the X-ray, the film itself, on the screen, but so as we can orientate ourselves if we could, please, Mr Murphy, go to tile 160.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's 161. Yes. It records an X-ray was taken at 00.27. If we just look at the description behind that tile, but not the X-ray itself, Mr Murphy. A radiological report made by a consultant radiologist colleague, Dr Boothroyd.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. She at the time was one of the two consultant radiologists, which are doctors who specialise in X-ray and
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: other image interpretation. She was one of the two in the hospital at the time who specialised in looking at our paediatric and neonatal X-rays.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Her description, does that in other language mirror the corresponding note that we've just been looking at from your clinical notes?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. So this is in more detail than my initial description because she would have reviewed the film on a high quality monitor the following day. She's put that the heart size is normal and the lungs are clear, which show that there is no indication, looking at the chest X-ray, why [Baby E]'s saturations were low. The tip of the ET tube, the breathing tube, lies just above the carina, which is where the windpipe splits into two and that's where the tube should be seen.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The tip of the nasogastric tube is projected over the region of the body of the stomach, which is just saying that it's in the stomach and in the right place.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then it moves on to the abdominal X-ray -- both of them were taken on the same X-ray because of the size of [Baby E]:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "The bowel gas pattern is within normal limits, with no evidence of intramural or free peritoneal gas."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Which shows that all -- the bowel should normally have gas in it and it looks normal and there was no evidence of any gas in either the bowel wall or outside the bowel wall, which are signs of NEC, and no evidence of bowel perforation, which means --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry, this is all going too quick. I am trying to make a summary note because you're saying a lot of quite important things here.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR C: Sorry.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We've dealt first with the nasogastric tube, which, in short, is appropriately placed?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So both tubes, the ETT and the NGT were in the right places?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Hence the successful respiration via both lungs?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The next entries deal with the abdominal X-ray --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- and the information derived therefrom. The first being the bowel gas pattern is within normal limits?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: With no evidence of intramural --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: That means gas within the bowel wall, which shouldn't be there, and is a sign of NEC if it is present.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that's the absence of an indicator of NEC?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The next and final clause in this sentence?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: "Free intra-peritoneal gas", which is gas that's come outside of the bowel, and again that's an indicator of NEC and is not present in this X-ray.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Pausing there, giving everyone a chance to digest that part of the note, and we move on. Is this a second independent fact or a related fact?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: It's a related fact that there's no evidence of bowel dilatation, which is when the bowel looks bigger and more swollen, which is also a sign of NEC, and that is also not present.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The final sentence?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: The left-sided peripheral long line, which is the intravenous line, is no longer evident on this image.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That was seen on one of the previous X-rays to confirm its position in the leg and had been withdrawn slightly because it was in an incorrect position and it wasn't visible on this X-ray because this X-ray didn't show his leg as much as the previous X-ray. So that's not a sign of a problem, it's just a sign that the line isn't visible on that X-ray.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So may we break that analysis up into three parts?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Essentially, the chest X-ray is normal with both tubes in a good position. The abdominal X-ray is also normal and the long line is not visible on the X-ray because the leg's not visible.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Mr Murphy, could we go back to tile 163 and the underlying note at J2558, [Dr C]'s note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We had got as far as looking at the X-ray and your summary of that information. Is anything on your note on that line that adds to that which you've just kindly taken us through?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: No.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. The next line, I think you began to tell us, relates to medication.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. I've written that [Baby E] was on "cef", which stands for cefotaxime, and "met", which stands for metronidazole. They are both intravenous antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that was a note of an existing provision of medication, was it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Does that relate back to Dr Harkness, or perhaps even before him?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I think -- I'm not sure but I think the cefotaxime had been started prior to that, but the metronidazole had been added in by Dr Harkness earlier that evening.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Others will assist in that regard in due course. I'm grateful. The second part of that entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: We'd planned to add in teicoplanin, a third antibiotic, which covers for skin bacteria because of the long line, the intravenous line being in place. Whenever you have plastic breaching the skin, you are at risk of getting infection from normal skin bacteria. Because [Baby E] had deteriorated we planned to add that in, but we had no chance to give that before further events unfolded.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that element of the plan was deferred because there were more pressing issues at hand; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So we go from the earlier part of your note. You estimate or approximate your arrival at 00.25?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Now we're 11 minutes on --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- or thereabouts at 00.36. What did you note and record there?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I've written that the oxygen saturations have dropped to 50 to 60%, still in 100% oxygen, and that [Baby E] has no detectable heart rate and that CPR, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, has been commenced.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Pausing there, is it right that this note details a significant deterioration?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did that deterioration occur when you were there?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I was on the neonatal unit, but I wasn't at [Baby E]'s cot side when that occurred, as far as I can remember.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you know where you were and what you were doing at that point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: When I'd arrived, the 11 minutes previously, I had initially gone to [Baby E]'s cot side, I'd had a handover from Dr Harkness and presumably from the nursing staff as well. We'd looked at [Baby E]'s fluid and observation charts that were with him. I'd examined him. But often, at night, in the nurseries, the lights are kept down fairly low to try and sort of avoid overstimulating the babies. So I think that Dr Harkness and I had gone to review [Baby E]'s blood results and to review his Xrays on the computer. We would have done that either at the nurses' station, which is outside of nursery 1, or there was a computer in nursery 1, but it was behind a pillar from where [Baby E]'s cot side was. I think at the time we were looking at information on the computer.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So you would have been either in a different part of nursery 1 or on the corridor just outside of nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the focus still on [Baby E], or [Baby E]'s data and his X-rays, but not cot side?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you recall where [Baby E] was placed at this point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: He was in nursery 1. There was a cot space. When you enter the neonatal unit through the double doors there was then -there were two doors into nursery 1, but the first door was directly in front of you when you entered the neonatal unit. He was in the cot side first on the right, which backed on to the wall of labour ward.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. From the point of the computer within nursery 1, as the room was configured at that point in time, are you able to say whether or not you had a line of sight from your position at the computer to [Baby E]'s cot?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: No, I wouldn't have been able to see his cot directly without sort of peering round the pillar.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And what if, to use your other alternative, you were at the computer at the nursing station?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I wouldn't have been able to see in the nursery at all.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you recall when and how you first learnt of this deterioration?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: No, I don't recall.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What is your first memory of these immediate events?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I can remember [Baby E] having CPR. I can remember Dr Harkness was doing the ventilation through the ET tube. Because he'd put that tube in, although the position looked good on the X-ray, I checked that myself using a laryngoscope just to look that it's in the correct position and that it hadn't become dislodged or fallen out because that would be a fixable cause for his deterioration.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Other than that, I was the team leader for the resuscitation and I try and avoid, as far as possible, doing physical tasks because you become fixated -- not fixated but you concentrate on the task that you're doing and you lose overall awareness of the situation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I was stood by [Baby E]'s cot with my back to the door, giving an overview and controlling the management while the resuscitation took place.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And the resuscitation team were led by Dr Harkness, is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Dr Harkness was doing the airway and the ventilation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I do remember Caroline Oakley doing chest compressions at least at one point, but often the nurses will rotate that to make sure that they don't get tired, and then Belinda, who was at the time Belinda Simcock, and Lucy Letby, were doing the drug medicines.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. We heard yesterday from a trainee, a junior doctor at the time, SHO, Dr Wood, and he took us yesterday, for your information, through his scribed contemporaneous notes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And did you subsequently rely upon those notes to assist you in the compilation of these notes of yours that we're looking at?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. So he was by the work surface that was sort of against the pillar and directly opposite [Baby E]'s cot and he was taking notes throughout of the timings and what we were doing.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So we'll look at the detail of the next listed events and then I'll invite you to give us a summary of your appreciation of the resuscitative attempts at this point.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You've already informed us, I think, that Dr Harkness confirmed the position --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I think I confirmed that.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You did, forgive me. So the ET was in a satisfactory position?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The air entry was good and remained bilateral?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Both lungs?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: And I've written "throughout". I would have checked that periodically, every few minutes throughout the resuscitation, just to check that the ET tube continues to be working well and hasn't dislodged or become blocked at any point.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So is it right that in doing that, you were seeking to check for, and if necessary eliminate, any mechanical obstructions, effectively?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. We want to make sure that the resuscitation that we're doing is good quality resuscitation to give [Baby E] the best possible chance, so want to make sure that there aren't any mechanical difficulties with the ventilation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Were there in this case?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: No. I haven't documented any and I don't remember any.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Next five entries. What is that list, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: This is a summary of the drugs and medicines that were given to [Baby E]. He had five doses of adrenaline, which is a standard resuscitation drug. It's normally given every 4 minutes during a resuscitation. He had two doses of bicarb. This is sodium bicarbonate and it's a medicine that helps correct acidosis because while a baby doesn't have adequate perfusion they can't get rid of acid from the body, so their blood becomes more acidotic.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you slow down a little through this? You've taken us through the adrenaline. You didn't, I don't think, tell us the purpose of that, although it might be self --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's a normal resuscitative drug?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: To stimulate the heart, is it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR C: It stimulates the heart and also helps preserve blood flow going to the brain and less to the peripheries where it's less needed.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Were you in a position to make a clinical judgement as to what, if any, effect that, the adrenaline, was having on [Baby E]?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I think initially it had no effect. I think later on we did see his heart rate briefly return following the adrenaline but I'm not 100% sure on that.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The introduction of the bicarb, is that capable of yielding any results or any signs of whether that's being effective in any way or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Not really. It's trying to correct any acidosis, but the only way to check that is by measuring a blood gas and it's very hard to do that when the baby has no blood circulation. So we don't routinely do that during a resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Next you've noted the introduction of dextrose.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: That's to correct if [Baby E] had a low blood sugar.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Again, we wouldn't measure that during the resuscitation because of the practical difficulties but it's again a standard resuscitation drug.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The next entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: [Baby E]'s had 20ml per kg of O negative blood. That was aiming to correct any blood loss or any fluid loss that may have occurred.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is there any means or was there any test or measure undertaken at the time to see whether that is in any way --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: We did check a blood gas, which also had a haemoglobin, a blood count level, later, but we didn't check that at the time, again for the practical reason.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. The last entry in this list?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: He's also had a 10ml per kg fluid bolus, which would have been saline, a salt solution, again in case a lack of circulating volume, blood volume or -- was contributing to his collapse.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that's a list of -- you had introduced to the baby as part of the attempts to resuscitate him.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In general terms, what, if any, effect were your efforts having?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: So initially, no effects at all, but we then did get a detectable heart rate from 01.01.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is this recorded in your next entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Take us through that please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: We then did get a detectable, recordable heart rate.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's high -- if a heart rate is above 60 we normally stop doing chest compressions, but it's less than 100, which is a less than ideal heart rate, he's still not breathing at that point, so IPPV is intermittent positive pressure ventilation, which is the
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did you and your colleagues withdraw to allow the family some privacy?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: I would imagine that we would do that. That would be usual practice.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Following the death of a patient, a neonate, do certain formalities have to be observed, [Dr C]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Yes. So anyone who dies needs to have a death certificate issued by a doctor and in order to do that you have to know the cause of death. Anyone who dies unexpectedly, which in medical terms means a death that you wouldn't have predicted 24 hours in advance -- and at the time all neonatal deaths on our unit were discussed with the coroner.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: At the time I felt that [Baby E] had NEC, which had led to his collapse and deterioration. So I discussed that with the coroner and we agreed for that to be put as [Baby E]'s cause of death.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What was it that drove you to that conclusion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Things that I was -- I didn't consider them fully at the time, but the fact that [Baby E]'s observations were very stable right up until the point of collapse doesn't fit with NEC. Normally we'd expect a deterioration where observations get worse over a period of hours, if not longer, prior to deterioration, and the abdominal X-ray not showing clear signs of NEC only an hour before he died -- sometimes signs on X-rays do take longer to develop, but if NEC was severe enough to cause circulatory collapse and a cardiac arrest then I would expect to see clear signs on an X-ray and I don't think I gave that enough weight at the time, that that X-ray had been normal.

blocks.text: DR C: Yes.

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You said "that was". What's the "that" in that sentence?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: NEC, sorry. That NEC was the most likely cause of a GI bleed in a baby of his gestation and clinical condition.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't think that now for the other factors that I've mentioned.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: to make what was a terrible situation for them any worse, so I didn't push the issue, which is something I now regret.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR C: Correct.
